meta.title: Durable Agents with Workflow Engines
meta.thesis: Durable Agents with Workflow Engines is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: An insurance-claims agent must survive retries, approval waits, and worker restarts. By the end, they should be able to build or review durable workflow state chart for a claims-processing agent, measure recovered workflow rate after restart, and catch the failure where the process loses its place after a tool timeout.

mentalMap.title: Durable Agents with Workflow Engines: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Use durable workflow engines when agent work must survive crashes, retries, timers, approvals, and long-running side effects.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Durable execution gives agent workflows replayable progress; it is a reliability layer underneath model calls, not a smarter model.

modules.title: Agents need more than a queue when work is long-lived
modules.sub: Durability matters when progress must survive failure.
modules.summary: A durable workflow remembers what already happened.
objectives: Explain why queues are not always enough.
Name agent tasks that need durable progress.
Separate reliability layer from LLM reasoning layer.

blocks.title: Durable execution is reliability for multi-step work

spans.text: Problem anchor: an agent drafts a compliance report, asks a human for approval, waits overnight, then files it in a vendor portal. If the worker restarts after approval, it must not repeat the earlier email or forget the approval.

A normal queue can retry a failed job, but durable workflow engines record progress so completed steps can be skipped and waiting states can resume. The LLM remains one activity inside a larger reliable process.
If a crash after step 4 would be expensive or confusing, design durable state before shipping.

blocks.analogy: A durable workflow is a trail of breadcrumbs the runtime can replay after the worker wakes up.

blocks.title: Case study: report approval over two days

spans.text: The workflow schedules a planning activity, runs retrieval, drafts a report, waits for a manager signal, and only then publishes. The event history records that planning and drafting already completed.
When a worker deploy happens during the wait, the workflow resumes at the approval point rather than starting over.

items.text: Identify external side effects and waits.
Split model/tool calls into named activities or steps.
Persist workflow state and approval signals.
Resume from the next unfinished step after failure.

blocks.title: Durability fit
blocks.prompt: Which task most clearly needs durable execution?

options.text: A multi-step agent that waits for human approval before sending a customer-facing report.
A calculator call inside one request.

blocks.explanation: Long waits and external side effects need recoverable progress.

modules.title: Workflow code owns control; activities own side effects
modules.sub: Replay works only when boundaries are clean.
modules.summary: Workflow/activity separation is the core durable design move.
objectives: Define workflow, activity, worker, and event history.

blocks.title: Replay demands deterministic orchestration

spans.text: Temporal-style systems replay workflow code from event history to rebuild state. That code must make the same decisions when given the same history. Randomness, current time, direct network calls, and model calls belong in activities or recorded side-effect boundaries.
Activities call models, APIs, databases, and tools. Because activities can retry after partial success, they need idempotency keys and clear timeout/retry policies.
If a line of code can send money, email, or mutate a database, it should not run as unguarded workflow logic.

blocks.analogy: The workflow is the conductor; activities are the musicians who make sound in the world.

options.name: Workflow

cells.text: Control flow, timers, waits, decisions from recorded state.

options.whenToUse: Use for orchestration and state transitions.

cells.text: Model call, API call, DB write, email, browser action.

options.name: In-memory loop
options.whenToUse: Use only for short noncritical tasks.

blocks.title: Boundary check
blocks.prompt: Where should an LLM API call usually live in a durable workflow?

options.text: Inside an activity or durable step with retry and timeout policy.
Only in the final UI renderer.

blocks.explanation: Model calls are nondeterministic external effects.

modules.title: Timers, signals, approvals, and retries shape the run
modules.sub: Durable agents wait and recover explicitly.
modules.summary: Durable workflows turn waiting into first-class state.
objectives: Use signals or events for approvals.
Set retry and timeout policy by activity risk.

blocks.title: Waiting is a durable state, not a sleeping thread

spans.text: A human approval may arrive hours later. A vendor API may rate limit until tomorrow. A model provider may fail transiently. Durable engines represent these as timers, signals, events, retries, and updates rather than a process sleeping in memory.
Retry policy should reflect side effects. A read-only retrieval step can retry more freely than a payment or email step. Timeouts protect cost and operator attention.
Every wait should have a timeout, escalation, or cancellation path.

blocks.analogy: Durable timers are calendar entries in the runtime, not a nap on one machine.

spans.text: A lesson publishing workflow drafts content, sends an approval packet, and waits for an `approve` or `request_changes` signal. The signal becomes part of event history.
If approval is denied, the workflow records cancellation. If changes are requested, it schedules a revision activity with the reviewer notes.

items.text: Create an approval packet with exact artifact and risk.
Wait for an approval signal with timeout.
Branch to publish, revise, or cancel.

blocks.title: Waiting model
blocks.prompt: Why is a durable signal better than polling a prompt for approval?

options.text: It records the external approval event and lets the workflow resume after crashes or deploys.
It forces all tasks to run forever.

blocks.explanation: Approvals are external events that durable workflows can persist.

modules.title: Implement idempotent step replay
modules.sub: A toy log shows why completed work should not repeat.
objectives: Predict which steps rerun after failure.
Use idempotency keys for side effects.

blocks.title: The history decides what to skip

spans.text: A durable runtime records successful commands and activity results. On recovery, it replays enough workflow logic to know which work is already done and what should happen next.
Spaced recall: from safety, retries of non-idempotent actions can duplicate side effects. Durable workflows reduce that risk only when activities are designed with idempotency.
A publish activity should include an idempotency key such as workflow ID plus step name.

blocks.title: Tiny durable-step simulator
blocks.code:
history = {"plan": "plan-v1"}  # imagine this survived a crash

def run_step(name, fn):
    if name in history:
        print("skip", name)
        return history[name]
    result = fn()
    history[name] = result
    print("record", name)
    return result

def call_model():
    return "draft-v1"

def publish():
    return {"published": True, "idempotency_key": "wf42:publish"}

plan = run_step("plan", lambda: "plan-v2")
draft = run_step("draft", call_model)
result = run_step("publish", publish)
print(plan, draft, result)
blocks.explanation: The simulator skips the completed plan step and records later steps, mirroring the durable idea without a real workflow engine.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict whether `plan-v2` replaces the recorded plan.
predictThenReveal.answer: It does not. The history already contains `plan`, so recovery uses `plan-v1` and continues with draft and publish.

blocks.title: Replay intuition
blocks.prompt: Why does durable replay skip an already completed activity?

options.text: The recorded history says the step succeeded, so rerunning it could duplicate side effects.

blocks.explanation: Event history is the source of recovery truth.

modules.title: Operate histories, versions, and cost
modules.summary: Reliable agent workflows need versioning, retention, and observability.
objectives: Avoid storing secrets and bloated prompts in history.
Monitor retries, cost, and stuck approvals.

spans.text: Event histories, step outputs, approval packets, and model responses are application data. They may contain PII, secrets, or large prompts if the workflow is careless. Store digests or references where possible and apply retention rules.

Long-lived workflows also need versioning discipline. Code changes should not break runs that started under an older control path. Operators need to distinguish workflow replay errors, activity errors, worker outages, and policy blocks.
Every durable agent run should expose status, last completed step, waiting reason, retry count, and cost budget.

blocks.title: Verify AI output from a durable agent workflow

spans.text: Review the workflow trace and final answer together.

items.text: Completed side-effecting steps are idempotent and not repeated after retry.
Human approvals are stored as explicit signals with artifact and reviewer.
Model calls have timeouts, retry budgets, and cost limits.
Event history avoids secrets, huge prompts, and unnecessary PII.
Operators can inspect stuck, failed, waiting, and cancelled states.

blocks.title: Operational risk
blocks.prompt: What is a common durable-workflow mistake for LLM apps?

options.text: Storing large prompts, secrets, or sensitive model outputs directly in long-lived histories.

blocks.explanation: Durable state needs the same privacy and retention discipline as other product data.

agent.label: Agent
agent.laymanDefinition: A software loop that plans, observes results, and may use tools to pursue a goal.
agent.technicalNote: Agent designs need explicit loop boundaries, stop conditions, permissions, state contracts, and evaluation surfaces before autonomy is useful.

tool.label: Tool
tool.laymanDefinition: An external capability the model can request, such as search, code execution, retrieval, or a business API.
tool.technicalNote: Tools require schemas, authorization, error handling, audit logs, and tests because natural-language intent is not execution permission.

state.label: State
state.laymanDefinition: The working information carried between steps of an agent workflow.
state.technicalNote: State should separate durable facts, transient scratch work, approvals, tool results, and failure metadata so retries and handoffs remain understandable.

memory.label: Memory
memory.laymanDefinition: Information saved across turns or sessions for future use.
memory.technicalNote: Agent memory needs scope, freshness, deletion, privacy controls, and evaluation so saved context helps rather than silently steering behavior.

mcp.label: MCP
mcp.laymanDefinition: A protocol for exposing tools and context to models and agent clients.
mcp.technicalNote: MCP-style integrations still need capability design, trust boundaries, lifecycle handling, and authorization around each exposed server.

sandbox.label: Sandbox
sandbox.laymanDefinition: An isolated environment that limits what agent actions can reach or change.
sandbox.technicalNote: Sandboxing should constrain files, network, processes, credentials, browser sessions, time, and side effects according to the task risk.
